scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In 1957, Dick Clark watched teenagers on American Bandstand transform the 19th-century Virginia Reel into a slow-drag rock 'n' roll promenade that would later become the iconic Soul Train Line.
This is The Stroll. Late 1950s.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (UrGLNtZ0rEg)
Title card: The Stroll · United States · Late 1950s

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Stroll gained national prominence in late 1957, with Billboard predicting its status as a major dance craze.
It was popularized through American Bandstand, where it was first danced to Chuck Willis's 'C. C. Rider.' Dick Clark noted its structural roots in the Virginia Reel, a much older folk dance.
The Diamonds' 1957 hit 'The Stroll' solidified its place in the rock 'n' roll canon.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Stroll served as a social mixer, allowing for individual couple display within a group setting.
It represented a shift toward slower, more stylized movement in teenage social dancing.
In later decades, it became a symbol of 1950s nostalgia and evolved into a showcase for urban dance styles on Soul Train.
Today it is a revived tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Down And Dirty: The Contemporary Versions Of The Great All Time Dances! [Full VHS] (https://archive.org/details/down-and-dirty-the-contemporary-versions-of-the-great-all-time-dances-full-vhs)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form two parallel lines, men on one side and women on the other, facing each other.
The lines move in place to the rhythm.
The couple at the head of the line joins hands and travels down the center 'aisle' between the lines, performing more complex or 'elaborate' steps before joining the end of the line.
Watch for The Promenade.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (UrGLNtZ0rEg)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Two parallel lines creating a central corridor or 'aisle'.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to slow rock 'n' roll and rhythm and blues.
Key instruments include the electric guitar, saxophone, and drums, often featuring a heavy, slow backbeat.
Listen for the Electric guitar, Saxophone, Drums, Piano.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 90 beats a minute.
A mid-tempo rock 'n' roll sound characterized by a walking bassline and a prominent, echoing snare. The music feels 'heavy' and deliberate, inviting a slow, swaying motion rather than fast footwork.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: The Stroll — The Diamonds; C. C. Rider — Chuck Willis; Rumble — Link Wray
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Slow, steady backbeat with a heavy emphasis on beats 2 and 4

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Originally performed in 1950s social settings such as high school gymnasiums, record hops, and television studios.
Typical attire of the era included poodle skirts, cardigans, and saddle shoes for women, and slacks with button-down shirts or leather jackets for men.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dick Clark is credited with popularizing the dance on American Bandstand.
The Diamonds provided its most famous musical accompaniment.
The most significant variant is the 'Soul Train Line,' which utilized the same two-line promenade structure but incorporated faster, more contemporary soul and funk movements.
The dance is structurally descended from the Virginia Reel.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: The Stroll is parent of Virginia Reel: The Stroll uses the same two-line facing formation and center promenade structure.
The Stroll is variant of Soul Train Line: A later adaptation of the format for soul and funk music.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Form two lines facing each other (men on one side, women on the other)
Step 2: Step-touch or sway in place to the slow beat
Footwork from the sources: In the lines: side-to-side step-touches. In the center: stylized walking, often with a 'drag' or 'slide' feel.
Drill: Step-touch to the left on counts 1-2
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: The lead couple meets in the center at the top of the line
Step 4: The couple travels down the center aisle with stylized walking or 'elaborate' steps
Drill: Step-touch to the right on counts 3-4
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Add a finger snap on the touch
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full
